why the half-interval is a WHOLE number of microseconds
THE BIT PERIOD IS 4 us: TWO 2 us HALF-INTERVALS.
And that is not tidiness. The decoder TIMESTAMPS the level on the 1 us counter
and compares it with the level recorded at the last CHANGE, and
is only exact if every transition lands on a tick. A bit period that is not a
multiple of the counter's unit would make the decoder's OWN ARITHMETIC the least
accurate thing in the act - and a decoder whose timing is its weakest part is not
a decoder that has been measured, it is one that has been assumed.

WHY THE BIT IS DECIDED ONCE PER BIT AND NOT ONCE PER
A bit is TWO half-intervals, so counting transitions and calling each one a bit
gives two bits where there is one. And the distinction that matters -
transition INSIDE a bit - is only visible if the decoder is counting
half-intervals rather than edges, because an edge is an edge wherever it falls.
dmem[8] counts half-intervals and dmem[12,13] holds the bit under construction.
the enabled-flag trap, which is the sixth of its kind
PINOE = 0x00 RELEASES EVERY PAD, AND IN PARTICULAR THE INPUT.
A pad the firmware DRIVES reads back its own register through PIN, not the wire.
Claiming the input pad means the firmware never sees the stream at all.
The first version of this init CLAIMED the input - writing BMC_IN to PINOE, on the
reasoning that "the input is the device's, so claim it" - and the symptom was that
, which reads as a decoder that does not work
rather than as an enable written backwards.
It is the SIXTH time in this block that a level and an enable have been
confused, and the only reason it was found at all is that the testbench's
check NAMES THE FLAG and the flag was 0xFF.
the one input the act must be able to FAIL on
A LINE HELD CONSTANT IS THE INPUT THAT MATTERS MOST.
bit of a well-formed frame carries a transition in its middle,

THAT is the stream the last check presents, and the firmware's answer to it must be
DECLARED FAILURE (dmem[3] = 0xFF) rather than a byte it invented.
A DECODER THAT CANNOT FAIL IS NOT A DECODER.
